selectionAlgorithm.description: Deterministic scoring: sum(signal_match * weight) for activation conditions. Inhibitors = hard reject (-Infinity). Return top N per category with score > 0.
priorityRules: Inhibitors are absolute — one firing kills the technique
Higher activation score wins ties within same category
PatternBreak re-runs selection with break-adjusted signal values
Voice Signature modifies technique EXECUTION, not selection

anchors.0.00: Pure emotion/story — zero data, zero evidence, zero logic Example: Nike "Just Do It" brand anthem — feeling IS the message
anchors.0.25: Minimal data — one statistic or fact, mostly narrative Example: Charity appeal with "1 in 5 children..." opener then all story
anchors.0.50: Balanced — arguments supported by evidence but wrapped in story Example: TED talk mixing personal anecdote with research citations
anchors.0.75: Evidence-led — structure built around data, story as seasoning Example: Consulting firm case study: metrics → methodology → results
anchors.1.00: Pure logic — densely evidenced, no emotional appeals Example: SEC filing, API documentation, research paper abstract

signals.grounding: Aristotle's logos — rational persuasion through logical argument (Rhetoric, ~330 BCE)

anchors.0.00: Deliberately unemotional — clinical, procedural, dry by design Example: Legal contract, assembly instructions, tax form guidance
anchors.0.25: Light emotional coloring — professional warmth without manipulation Example: Corporate annual letter acknowledging team effort
anchors.0.50: Emotionally engaged — genuine feeling woven through substance Example: Product launch that connects features to human outcomes
anchors.0.75: Emotion-forward — audience should FEEL before they THINK Example: Nonprofit campaign video, memorial tribute, Nike "Dream Crazy"
anchors.1.00: Raw emotional immersion — tears, rage, euphoria, awe Example: ASPCA Sarah McLachlan spot, grief memoir, war correspondence, charity: water origin film

signals.grounding: Aristotle's pathos — emotional persuasion through audience affect (Rhetoric, ~330 BCE)

anchors.0.00: No authority claim — content stands on its own merit Example: Anonymous Reddit post, crowdsourced wiki entry
anchors.0.25: Implied credibility — brand reputation does the work, no explicit claims Example: Apple product page — authority is assumed, never stated
anchors.0.50: Moderate credentials — occasional references to expertise or track record Example: Blog post mentioning "in our 10 years of..." or citing industry experience
anchors.0.75: Credential-forward — expertise is a key persuasion lever Example: Doctor explaining a procedure, "as a Stanford researcher..."
anchors.1.00: Authority IS the message — the point is who's saying it Example: Expert testimony, peer-reviewed publication, celebrity endorsement

signals.grounding: Aristotle's ethos — persuasion through speaker credibility (Rhetoric, ~330 BCE)

anchors.0.00: Timeless — no urgency, no expiration, evergreen relevance Example: Brand manifesto, educational explainer, origin story
anchors.0.25: Soft relevance — topical but not urgent Example: "This season's trends" — relevant now, not panic-inducing
anchors.0.50: Moderate urgency — clear reason to act soon but not immediately Example: "Early bird pricing ends this month" — deadline but distant
anchors.0.75: High urgency — specific deadline, clear consequence of inaction Example: "48-hour flash sale", "Applications close Friday"
anchors.1.00: Extreme pressure — act NOW or lose permanently Example: "Last 3 tickets", "Offer expires at midnight", crisis communications

signals.grounding: Aristotle's kairos — the opportune moment for persuasion; Cialdini's scarcity principle

anchors.0.00: Zero thinking required — content is consumed passively Example: Background music playlist description, ambient video caption
anchors.0.25: Minimal processing — familiar concepts, no new mental models Example: Recipe card, simple how-to, motivational quote card
anchors.0.50: Moderate engagement — audience follows an argument or learns something Example: Explainer video, product comparison, feature walkthrough
anchors.0.75: Active thinking — audience must connect ideas, apply frameworks Example: Strategy whitepaper, investment thesis, complex tutorial
anchors.1.00: Deep cognitive work — audience builds new mental models Example: Academic lecture, philosophy essay, systems architecture doc

signals.grounding: Petty & Cacioppo's Elaboration Likelihood Model — central vs peripheral processing

anchors.remember: Audience recalls facts — "Nike was founded in 1964"
anchors.understand: Audience grasps meaning — "Nike's direct-to-consumer shift changed retail"
anchors.apply: Audience uses knowledge — "Here's how to structure your pitch like Nike"
anchors.analyze: Audience breaks down components — "Why Nike's strategy works: 3 pillars"
anchors.evaluate: Audience makes judgments — "Is Nike's approach right for YOUR brand?"
anchors.create: Audience produces something new — "Design your own brand strategy using this framework"

signals.grounding: Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl 2001)

anchors.0.00: Confirming — audience already knows everything; content validates Example: Brand ad reinforcing existing perception, company values page
anchors.0.25: Mostly familiar — one new angle on a known topic Example: "5 things you didn't know about coffee" (4 are known, 1 is new)
anchors.0.50: Half new — meaningful new information mixed with context-setting Example: Product launch with both familiar brand + genuinely new features
anchors.0.75: Mostly new — audience is learning significantly Example: First exposure to a new technology, paradigm-shifting research
anchors.1.00: Completely new — audience has no prior framework Example: Announcing a category that didn't exist, groundbreaking discovery

signals.grounding: Shannon's information theory — surprise as information content

anchors.0.00: Hyper-concrete — specific things, people, places, actions Example: "Sarah picked up the 2023 MacBook Air in Midnight and clicked Buy"
anchors.0.25: Mostly concrete — tangible examples with occasional generalization Example: Product demo showing specific UI screens and clicks
anchors.0.50: Mixed — concrete examples illustrating abstract principles Example: "Innovation means [abstract] — like when we built [concrete example]"
anchors.0.75: Mostly abstract — principles and frameworks with sparse examples Example: Strategy document about market positioning
anchors.1.00: Pure abstraction — concepts, theories, universal principles Example: "Excellence is the margin between effort and expectation"

signals.grounding: Hayakawa's Abstraction Ladder (Language in Thought and Action, 1949)

anchors.0.00: No sensory/gut reaction — purely intellectual content Example: Tax filing instructions, API changelog
anchors.0.25: Mild aesthetic appeal — pleasant but not arresting Example: Airbnb listing description, cafe menu copy
anchors.0.50: Noticeable impact — audience pauses, reacts physically Example: Apple product reveal slow-mo, "shot on iPhone" gallery
anchors.0.75: Strong visceral hit — sharp intake of breath, goosebumps, flinch Example: Nike "Dream Crazy" Kaepernick opening, Volvo truck splits Jean-Claude Van Damme
anchors.1.00: Overwhelming — shock, awe, visceral discomfort, can't look away Example: Dumb Ways to Die, Thai life insurance ads, "Most Shocking Second a Day" (Save the Children)

signals.grounding: Norman's visceral design level (Emotional Design, 2004)

anchors.0.00: Zero actionability — content is for feeling or knowing, not doing Example: Brand anthem, origin story, art film
anchors.0.25: Vague inspiration — "you should try this" without specifics Example: Motivational LinkedIn post, TED talk closing call-to-action
anchors.0.50: Moderate utility — clear takeaways but audience must figure out details Example: "5 strategies for better sleep" — direction without prescription
anchors.0.75: Highly actionable — step-by-step, immediately applicable Example: Notion template walkthrough, HubSpot marketing playbook
anchors.1.00: Tool-like — content IS the action (template, checklist, calculator) Example: Canva template, ROI calculator landing page, Typeform quiz

signals.grounding: Norman's behavioral design level — usability and function satisfaction

anchors.0.00: No lasting impression — consumed and forgotten Example: Product spec sheet, shipping notification, weather update
anchors.0.25: Mild reflection — audience thinks about it briefly after Example: Interesting LinkedIn insight, "huh, I didn't know that" blog post
anchors.0.50: Genuine pause — audience reconsiders an assumption or belief Example: Patagonia "Don't Buy This Jacket" — rethinks consumption
anchors.0.75: Deep impact — content changes how audience sees a topic Example: "An Inconvenient Truth", Dove "Real Beauty Sketches"
anchors.1.00: Worldview shift — audience questions fundamental beliefs Example: "13th" documentary, "Pale Blue Dot" (Carl Sagan)

signals.grounding: Norman's reflective design level — self-image and meaning-making

anchors.0.00: Zero immersion — audience fully aware they are reading/watching content Example: Terms of service, form instructions, compliance notice
anchors.0.25: Light engagement — audience follows along but mind wanders Example: Standard corporate blog, routine newsletter
anchors.0.50: Moderate absorption — audience is engaged, occasionally pulled out Example: Good podcast episode, well-written case study
anchors.0.75: Deep immersion — audience loses track of time, emotionally invested Example: Serial podcast, Humans of New York stories, long-form New Yorker profile
anchors.1.00: Complete transportation — audience forgets they are consuming media Example: "The Bear" opening sequence, Pixar "Up" first 10 minutes, Ira Glass at his best

signals.grounding: Green & Brock's transportation theory (2000) — narrative absorption reduces counter-arguing

anchors.-1.0: Dark, tragic, grief — "We lost everything in the fire"
anchors.-0.5: Somber, serious, concerned — "The numbers are alarming"
anchors.0.0: Neutral — factual, balanced, neither positive nor negative
anchors.+0.5: Warm, hopeful, encouraging — "Things are getting better"
anchors.+1.0: Euphoric, celebratory, triumphant — "We did it! Record-breaking!"

signals.grounding: Russell's circumplex model of affect — valence axis (1980)

anchors.0.00: Complete calm — meditative, ASMR, deliberately soporific
anchors.0.25: Low-key — conversational, relaxed, unhurried
anchors.0.50: Engaged — alert and interested, normal presentation energy
anchors.0.75: Intense — elevated heart rate, leaning forward, urgent Example: Product launch countdown, competitive sports narration, crisis update
anchors.1.00: Peak arousal — fight-or-flight intensity (loud OR quiet: explosive MrBeast energy AND sustained quiet dread of a cancer diagnosis scene both live here. Arousal ≠ volume.) Example: MrBeast "$1 vs $1,000,000" reveal (loud peak), Moonlight diner scene (quiet peak)

signals.grounding: Russell's circumplex model — arousal axis, independent of valence

anchors.unaware: Doesn't know the problem exists — need pattern interrupt
anchors.problem_aware: Knows the problem, not the solution — need education
anchors.solution_aware: Knows solutions exist, hasn't chosen — need differentiation
anchors.product_aware: Knows your product, hasn't bought — need conviction
anchors.most_aware: Existing customer — need retention, upsell, advocacy

signals.grounding: Eugene Schwartz's 5 Levels of Awareness (Breakthrough Advertising, 1966)

anchors.0.00: Zero domain knowledge — explain everything, no jargon
anchors.0.25: Basic familiarity — knows the field exists, needs hand-holding
anchors.0.50: Working knowledge — can follow industry discussion, skip basics
anchors.0.75: Expert — deep domain knowledge, skip to advanced concepts
anchors.1.00: Peer expert — assume complete mastery, use full jargon

signals.grounding: Cognitive load theory — extraneous load from unnecessary explanation

anchors.0.00: Zero social proof — content stands on logic/emotion alone
anchors.0.25: Light social proof — occasional mention of others ("many companies...")
anchors.0.50: Moderate — testimonials, case studies, or numbers woven in
anchors.0.75: Heavy reliance — "10,000 customers", named brands, specific results
anchors.1.00: Social proof IS the content — entire piece is testimonials/reviews

signals.grounding: Cialdini's social proof principle (Influence, 1984)

anchors.0.00: Universal — zero insider references, accessible to anyone
anchors.0.25: Light shared context — occasional reference insiders appreciate
anchors.0.50: Moderate tribalism — "if you know, you know" moments
anchors.0.75: Strong insider language — jargon, references that exclude outsiders
anchors.1.00: Fully tribal — incomprehensible to non-members, deliberately exclusive

signals.grounding: Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner 1979) — in-group/out-group bonding through shared language

anchors.0.00: Full direction — "Do this. Now." No choice offered.
anchors.0.25: Guided — "We recommend this approach" — one option with reason
anchors.0.50: Options — "Here are three approaches, each with tradeoffs"
anchors.0.75: Open — "Consider these factors and decide what's right for you"
anchors.1.00: Full autonomy — "Here's what we know. You take it from here."

signals.grounding: Deci & Ryan's Self-Determination Theory (2000) — autonomy as intrinsic motivation driver

anchors.0.00: Glacial — one idea explored for minutes, long pauses, meditation pace
anchors.0.25: Slow — deliberate, each point gets full development, documentary pace
anchors.0.50: Moderate — conversational flow, natural topic progression
anchors.0.75: Fast — rapid topic transitions, dense information delivery
anchors.1.00: Breakneck — idea every 2-3 seconds, no pause, TikTok/Reels pace

signals.grounding: Editing pacing research — cuts/min correlates with perceived energy. Extended to writing via ideas/paragraph density.

anchors.0.00: Flat — no tension, no buildup, no release. Informational only.
anchors.0.25: Gentle slope — mild curiosity, small question answered at end
anchors.0.50: Standard arc — clear setup, rising action, resolution
anchors.0.75: Strong arc — significant stakes, delayed payoff, emotional investment
anchors.1.00: Extreme tension — cliffhanger, unresolved, audience on edge

signals.grounding: Freytag's dramatic structure (Die Technik des Dramas, 1863); Duarte's Sparkline

anchors.0.00: Completely surprising — audience cannot anticipate what comes next
anchors.0.25: Mostly surprising — occasional familiar patterns, mostly unexpected
anchors.0.50: Balanced — familiar structure with surprising content (or vice versa)
anchors.0.75: Mostly predictable — audience knows the shape, enjoys the execution
anchors.1.00: Fully predictable — template content, audience knows exactly what's coming

signals.grounding: Information theory — surprise as information content. Predictability is not bad — it reduces cognitive load and builds trust. The question is whether the predictability is intentional.

anchors.0.00: Extremely simple — grade 3-4 level, basic vocabulary, short sentences
anchors.0.25: Simple — grade 6-8, everyday language, clear syntax
anchors.0.50: Moderate — grade 10-12, some complex sentences, standard vocabulary
anchors.0.75: Complex — college level, subordinate clauses, technical vocabulary
anchors.1.00: Highly complex — academic/legal, dense syntax, specialized terminology

signals.grounding: Flesch-Kincaid readability formula. Note: reading level as a single number is an imperfect proxy — it captures syntax complexity but not conceptual difficulty. A Hemingway novel scores grade 4-7 on Flesch-Kincaid (varies by analysis method) but is not grade-school content.

anchors.-1.0: Irreverent — slang, broken rules, profanity-adjacent Example: Wendy's Twitter roasts, Cards Against Humanity packaging
anchors.-0.5: Casual — conversational, contractions, first-name basis Example: Mailchimp emails, Slack notifications
anchors.0.0: Neutral — neither formal nor casual, professional but approachable Example: Google blog posts, standard SaaS communications
anchors.+0.5: Formal — proper grammar, measured tone, institutional voice Example: McKinsey reports, university communications
anchors.+1.0: High formal — legal precision, ceremonial weight Example: Supreme Court opinions, diplomatic communications

signals.grounding: NN/g's 4-dimension tone model — formality axis. Merged with original irreverence signal per Eng review.

anchors.0.00: Zero humor — dead serious, no levity of any kind
anchors.0.25: Dry wit — occasional clever phrasing, understated amusement
anchors.0.50: Clearly playful — audience smiles, lighthearted tone throughout
anchors.0.75: Comedy-forward — laughs are a primary goal alongside the message
anchors.1.00: Pure comedy — the joke IS the content

signals.grounding: NN/g tone model — humor axis. Humor in writing shares mechanisms with stand-up: setup, misdirection, payoff.

anchors.0.00: Flat affect — deliberately monotone, matter-of-fact
anchors.0.25: Measured — controlled energy, professional composure
anchors.0.50: Warm engagement — genuine interest without over-excitement
anchors.0.75: Energetic — exclamation marks earned, audible smile
anchors.1.00: Explosive — MrBeast energy, ALL CAPS justified, maximum hype

signals.grounding: NN/g tone model — enthusiasm axis

anchors.0.00: Cold professional — deliberate distance, institution speaking Example: Law firm client letter, IRS notice
anchors.0.25: Polite distance — courteous but impersonal Example: Standard corporate communications
anchors.0.50: Approachable — "we're people too" with professional boundaries Example: Salesforce blog, Notion documentation
anchors.0.75: Warm — personal, empathetic, mentor-like Example: Headspace copy, Patagonia essays
anchors.1.00: Intimate — feels like a close friend talking to you Example: Personal newsletter, handwritten founder letter

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — distinguishes cold professional (law firm) from warm mentor (Headspace). Not captured by formality alone — formal + warm = possible (university president's commencement speech).

anchors.teacher: "I know this and I'll explain it to you" — Masterclass, Khan Academy
anchors.peer: "We're figuring this out together" — indie newsletters, community posts
anchors.guide: "I've been where you are, let me show you the path" — Headspace, therapy apps
anchors.oracle: "Here is truth" — Kurzgesagt, The Economist, Apple keynotes

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — captures the knowledge-relationship between writer and audience. Vox = teacher, Kurzgesagt = oracle, 3Blue1Brown = co-discoverer.

anchors.0.00: Explicitly uncertain — "we don't know yet", "the data is unclear"
anchors.0.25: Hedged — "it appears that", "evidence suggests", "we believe"
anchors.0.50: Balanced — confident claims with acknowledged limitations
anchors.0.75: Confident — "this works", "here's what you should do"
anchors.1.00: Absolute certainty — "this IS the answer", zero qualification

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — startup pitch (certainty 0.9) vs scientific paper (certainty 0.4) vs Apple keynote (certainty 1.0).

anchors.forward: "The future is..." — startup pitches, innovation content, vision statements
anchors.present: "Right now..." — news, tutorials, product demos, current state descriptions
anchors.backward: "We've always..." — heritage brands, origin stories, nostalgia marketing

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — Nike (forward: "the future of sport") vs Patagonia (backward: "we've always believed") vs Apple (present: "this changes everything, today").

anchors.command: "Do this." — Nike "Just Do It", military recruitment, direct-response CTA
anchors.confide: "Between us..." — Personal newsletters, behind-the-scenes, vulnerable sharing
anchors.provoke: "Are you sure about that?" — Contrarian takes, challenger brands, thought leadership

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — power_dynamic + epistemic_stance together capture the full relationship between writer and audience.

anchors.0.00: Maximum understatement — says less than it means, trusts audience Example: Hemingway prose, Patagonia product descriptions
anchors.0.25: Restrained — measured delivery, occasional emphasis
anchors.0.50: Standard — emphasis matches content importance
anchors.0.75: Amplified — deliberate intensity, theatrical moments
anchors.1.00: Maximum performance — MrBeast, Gary Vee, preachers, stadium announcers

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — MrBeast (1.0) vs Casey Neistat (0.3) share similar enthusiasm but differ radically in intensity_performance.

anchors.0.00: Zero teaching — pure entertainment, emotion, or persuasion
anchors.0.25: Incidental learning — audience picks up facts along the way
anchors.0.50: Balanced — learning is a goal but not the only one
anchors.0.75: Education-primary — structure exists to teach effectively
anchors.1.00: Pure education — every sentence advances understanding

signals.grounding: Gagne's 9 Events of Instruction; Mayer's 12 Principles of Multimedia Learning

anchors.0.00: Zero entertainment value — utility content, compliance, reference
anchors.0.25: Mildly engaging — readable/watchable but pleasure is not the point
anchors.0.50: Genuinely enjoyable — audience would choose this over alternatives
anchors.0.75: Entertainment-primary — audience is here for the experience
anchors.1.00: Pure entertainment — content exists solely for pleasure/diversion

signals.grounding: Uses and Gratifications Theory (Katz, Blumler & Gurevitch, 1974)

anchors.0.00: No relational goal — content is transactional, one-directional
anchors.0.25: Light connection — "follow for more", mild community nod
anchors.0.50: Relationship-building — "we're in this together", shared values
anchors.0.75: Deep bonding — vulnerability, shared struggle, we-language
anchors.1.00: Pure connection — content exists to strengthen the relationship

signals.grounding: Deci & Ryan's relatedness need (SDT, 2000); parasocial relationship theory

anchors.0.00: Ephemeral — irrelevant within hours/days (trending topic, breaking news)
anchors.0.25: Short-lived — relevant for weeks (seasonal campaign, product launch)
anchors.0.50: Medium shelf life — relevant for months (quarterly report, feature release)
anchors.0.75: Long-lasting — relevant for years (brand manifesto, evergreen tutorial)
anchors.1.00: Timeless — relevant indefinitely (foundational principles, origin story)

signals.grounding: Content marketing lifecycle models; SEO evergreen vs topical content distinction

anchors.0.00: Hyper-narrow — one specific instance, person, or event
anchors.0.25: Narrow — one product, one company, one situation
anchors.0.50: Moderate — an industry, a demographic, a trend
anchors.0.75: Broad — a generation, a society, a movement
anchors.1.00: Universal — the human condition, nature, existence

signals.grounding: Journalism's scope ladder — from local incident to universal truth

anchors.0.00: No silence, no pauses, no white space — wall-to-wall content
anchors.0.25: Minimal breathing room — tight editing, dense but with paragraph breaks
anchors.0.50: Balanced — deliberate pauses, section breaks, room to digest
anchors.0.75: Generous space — let the audience sit with ideas, silence after key points
anchors.1.00: Space IS the content — Patagonia-style 60% silence, haiku minimalism

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "the taxonomy is entirely additive. Great writing is equally about what to LEAVE OUT." Musical rest theory — silence gives notes meaning.

anchors.0.00: Generic — "She drove a car"
anchors.0.25: Category-level — "She drove a hatchback"
anchors.0.50: Brand-level — "She drove a Volvo"
anchors.0.75: Model-level — "She drove a 1987 Volvo 240"
anchors.1.00: Hyper-specific — "She drove a 1987 Volvo 240 with a bobblehead of Ruth Bader Ginsburg on the dash"

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "single fastest way to make writing feel human." Concrete language activates more neural pathways than abstract (Jessen et al., 2000 — fMRI studies of concrete vs abstract words).

anchors.0.00: Metronomic — every sentence the same length and structure
anchors.0.25: Low variation — mostly similar with occasional change
anchors.0.50: Moderate — noticeable rhythm with intentional shifts
anchors.0.75: High variation — deliberate alternation between short punchy and long flowing
anchors.1.00: Maximum variation — "Short. Short. Then a sentence that unfurls like a flag in wind, clause after clause, building to something you didn't see coming." Hemingway meets Faulkner.

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "sentence length variation IS the craft." Prose rhythm research (Hye-Knudsen 2023 — rhythmic variation correlates with reader engagement).

anchors.0.00: No pivot — linear progression, no reversals
anchors.0.25: Gentle turn — subtle shift in perspective or argument
anchors.0.50: Clear pivot — "But here's the thing..." — audience feels the turn
anchors.0.75: Sharp reversal — "Everything I just said is wrong" — attention spike
anchors.1.00: Whiplash — complete 180, audience gasps, subverts all expectations

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "every great piece has a moment where it pivots. Not tension_arc (continuous). A discrete hinge."

anchors.0.00: No callbacks — each section is self-contained, no cross-references
anchors.0.25: Occasional echo — one moment references an earlier one
anchors.0.50: Regular callbacks — setup/payoff pairs every few sections
anchors.0.75: Dense callbacks — multiple threads planted and paid off, comedy-writer density
anchors.1.00: Everything connects — every element is both setup and payoff for something else

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "plant in minute 1, pay off in minute 8." Setup/payoff is fundamental to screenwriting (Robert McKee, Story, 1997).

anchors.0.00: Surface only — content means exactly what it says, no layers
anchors.0.25: Light subtext — occasional implications, mostly explicit
anchors.0.50: Moderate — surface meaning + an underlying message/theme
anchors.0.75: Rich subtext — multiple layers of meaning, rewards re-reading
anchors.1.00: Almost entirely subtextual — surface is a vehicle for deeper meaning

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "gap between surface meaning and intended meaning. Great writing operates on 2+ levels."

anchors.0.00: Fully explicit — everything stated directly, nothing left to inference
anchors.0.25: Mostly explicit — audience fills in small gaps
anchors.0.50: Balanced — some things said, some implied, audience is trusted
anchors.0.75: Heavily implied — audience constructs significant meaning
anchors.1.00: Almost nothing stated — reader does the heavy lifting

signals.grounding: Scriptwriter review — "great writing trusts the audience to construct meaning." Grice's Cooperative Principle and conversational implicature (1975).
Scriptwriter review + Copywriter review (6 additional types added in verification)

anchors.0.00: Audio-only friendly — content works with eyes closed Example: Podcast, audiobook, radio ad
anchors.0.25: Mostly verbal — occasional "as you can see" but visuals are supplementary Example: Talking head vlog, keynote with minimal slides
anchors.0.50: Balanced — narration and visuals carry equal weight Example: Tutorial with screen share, cooking video with voiceover
anchors.0.75: Visual-led — narration references specific visual elements constantly Example: Product demo, SaaS walkthrough, fashion lookbook
anchors.1.00: Purely visual — zero narration, visuals ARE the content Example: ASMR cooking, silent cinematic montage, animated infographic

signals.grounding: CEO review — "suspiciously text-only." Directly controls narration volume: low → dense VO, high → minimal/zero VO.

anchors.0.00: All tell — narrator describes everything ("Picture a golden sunset...")
anchors.0.25: Mostly tell — narration carries the story, visuals support
anchors.0.50: Balanced — narration sets up, visuals pay off
anchors.0.75: Mostly show — visuals lead, sparse narration punctuates
anchors.1.00: All show — product speaks for itself, words are minimal

signals.grounding: Screenwriting principle: "show, don't tell." Controls narration density — at 0.0, a 30s script needs ~75 words; at 1.0, it needs ~10 words or zero.

anchors.0.00: Perfect alignment — audio mirrors visual exactly ("click here" + arrow)
anchors.0.25: Complementary — same message, different information per channel
anchors.0.50: Layered — narration adds context visuals cannot show (backstory, feelings)
anchors.0.75: Deliberate tension — serene visuals + urgent narration, or vice versa
anchors.1.00: Full contradiction — channels say opposite things for artistic effect

signals.grounding: CEO review — needed for video company. Film theory: Eisenstein's montage theory (meaning from juxtaposition of contrasting elements). Patagonia brand films routinely use 0.7-0.8.

techniques.primary: Open with a question the audience already has but hasn't articulated. Not a generic question — a SPECIFIC question that proves you understand their situation.
techniques.complements: Follow with a brief credibility marker (ethos) before answering.
antiPatterns: Generic questions ("Want to grow your business?") — too broad, feels like spam
Questions with obvious answers — insulting to the audience
Multiple questions stacked — cognitive overload, pick ONE

weightResponse.elaboration > 0.7: philosophical question ("What if everything you know about X is wrong?")
weightResponse.elaboration 0.3-0.7: practical question ("How do you handle X when Y happens?")

techniques.why: Questions activate the brain's completion instinct (Zeigarnik effect). An unanswered question creates an open loop that the audience must close by continuing to read/watch.
techniques.example: "What happens to your brand when your best copywriter quits?" — specific, painful, relevant

techniques.primary: Open with a surprising data point that reframes the audience's understanding. The stat must be COUNTERINTUITIVE — confirming what people already believe is not a hook.
techniques.complements: Follow with "...and here's why that matters to you" (behavioral_utility bridge).
antiPatterns: Made-up or unverifiable statistics — destroys ethos instantly
Stats without source — feels like LLM fabrication (the #1 anti-AI tell)
Multiple stats in the hook — one is a hook, three is a data dump

weightResponse.logos > 0.8: lead with the number ("73% of..."), source immediately
weightResponse.logos 0.5-0.8: embed the stat in a narrative framing ("Most people assume X. The data says Y.")

techniques.why: Cognitive disruption — a counterintuitive fact creates a prediction error in the brain (Rescorla-Wagner model). The audience stays to resolve the discrepancy between what they believed and what the data shows.
techniques.example: "97% of video content gets zero organic reach. Here's what the 3% does differently."

techniques.primary: Open in the middle of a specific moment. Not backstory — a vivid, concrete scene that the audience enters immediately. "It was 3am and the server was on fire."
techniques.complements: Delay context — let the scene breathe before explaining why it matters.
antiPatterns: Starting with backstory ("Let me tell you about my journey...") — earned, not given
Vague scene-setting ("Imagine a world where...") — generic, not specific
Stories that are clearly manufactured for the content — audience detects inauthenticity

weightResponse.pathos > 0.8: start in the most emotionally intense moment (in medias res at the crisis)
weightResponse.pathos 0.5-0.8: start at a moment of tension or decision

techniques.why: Green & Brock transportation theory — a concrete scene activates narrative absorption, reducing the audience's counter-arguing defenses. They are IN the story before they decide whether to stay.
techniques.example: "She stared at the Slack notification. 47 unread messages. All from the same channel."

techniques.primary: Open with a bold, contrarian claim that challenges conventional wisdom. Must be defensible — not clickbait, but a genuine alternative perspective.
techniques.complements: Immediately signal that evidence is coming ("...and I can prove it.").
antiPatterns: Provocations you can't back up — damages ethos permanently
Insulting the audience ("You're doing it wrong") — provoke their assumptions, not their competence
Clickbait gap ("You won't BELIEVE...") — audience is trained to detect and punish this

weightResponse.certainty > 0.8: absolute statement ("X is dead. Here's what replaces it.")
weightResponse.certainty 0.6-0.8: qualified provocation ("The conventional wisdom about X is dangerously wrong.")

techniques.why: Cognitive dissonance — a confident claim that contradicts the audience's beliefs creates discomfort that can only be resolved by engaging with the argument. Berlyne's optimal arousal.
techniques.example: "Content calendars are killing your brand. Stop scheduling. Start responding."

techniques.primary: Open with something unexpected that STOPS the scroll — a jarring visual direction, a sentence fragment, a sound, a contradiction. The goal is the 0.4-second stopping reaction, not comprehension. Comprehension comes in the next 3 seconds.
techniques.complements: Follow immediately with context (within 2 sentences) or audience bounces.
antiPatterns: Shock without substance — stops the scroll but loses the audience at second 4
Pattern interrupts on every piece — audience builds tolerance fast
Interrupts that contradict the brand voice — jarring in the wrong way

weightResponse.pacing > 0.9: maximum disruption — fragment, visual, unexpected angle
weightResponse.pacing 0.7-0.9: moderate interruption — unexpected opening line, contrast

techniques.why: Orienting response (Sokolov 1963) — novel stimuli trigger involuntary attention.
techniques.example: "STOP. Before you read another productivity tip." (then pivots to a genuine insight)

techniques.primary: Open with the RESULT the audience wants, then explain how to get there. "Here's how we cut our CAC by 40% in 6 weeks." — destination first, journey second.
techniques.complements: Include a specificity marker (the number, the timeframe, the constraint).
antiPatterns: Vague outcomes ("grow your business") — no specificity = no hook
Outcomes the audience doesn't care about — must map to THEIR pain
Unbelievable outcomes without hedging — "10x your revenue in a week" triggers BS detector

weightResponse.behavioral > 0.8: specific number + timeframe + constraint in the hook

techniques.why: Outcome-first structure (product demo pattern from Part 5) applied to hooks. The audience evaluates effort-to-outcome ratio — showing the outcome first makes the effort worth evaluating.
techniques.example: "We reduced 12-hour video production to 45 minutes. Here's the exact workflow."

techniques.primary: Problem (name the pain) → Agitate (make it vivid) → Solve (present the answer). Works best under 60 seconds / 300 words. The agitation must be SPECIFIC — not "this is bad" but "here's exactly how this ruins your Tuesday."
antiPatterns: Agitation without empathy — making the audience feel stupid for having the problem
Weak agitation — "this is a challenge" instead of vivid, specific pain
Solution too early — jumping to solve before the audience feels the sting

weightResponse.kairos > 0.7: compressed PAS — problem and agitation in one sentence, jump to solve
weightResponse.kairos 0.3-0.7: full PAS — each phase gets development

techniques.why: Direct response copywriting's most proven structure (Dan Kennedy, Gary Halbert). Agitation bridges the gap between "I have a problem" and "I need to solve it NOW."
techniques.example: P: "Your onboarding takes 3 weeks." A: "That's 3 weeks of salary for every hire who can't contribute. 12 hires a year = 36 lost weeks." S: "One playbook. Day-one productive."

techniques.primary: Attention (hook) → Interest (relevance) → Desire (benefits) → Action (CTA). Classic funnel. Works best for 60s-3min content / 300-1000 words. Each stage must EARN the next — attention doesn't guarantee interest.
antiPatterns: Rushing through Interest to get to Desire — audience hasn't bought in yet
Desire section that is features-list instead of benefits — "we have X" vs "you get Y"
CTA disconnected from Desire — the action must feel like the natural next step

weightResponse.persuasion > 0.8: aggressive AIDA — each stage shorter, harder push toward action
weightResponse.persuasion 0.5-0.8: balanced AIDA — interest and desire get most of the time

techniques.why: St. Elmo Lewis (1898). Still works because it maps to the buyer's psychological journey.
techniques.example: A: "Your customers abandon carts 73% of the time." I: "Most recovery emails feel like spam." D: "Imagine a follow-up that sounds like a friend, not a bot." A: "Start your free trial."

techniques.primary: Alternate between "what is" (current reality) and "what could be" (vision) throughout the piece. Each swing builds amplitude until the final "what could be" becomes irresistible. Duarte's presentation structure.
antiPatterns: "What could be" too vague — audience needs to SEE the alternative, not just hear "imagine better"
Equal length swings — vary the rhythm, build amplitude (wider swings toward the end)
No final resolution — sparkline must end on "what could be" as the new reality

weightResponse.tension > 0.8: wide swings between is/could-be, dramatic contrast

techniques.why: Nancy Duarte's analysis of great presentations (Sparkline, 2010). The oscillation creates sustained engagement because the audience is never settled — always pulled between realities.
techniques.example: "Today, a junior designer waits 2 days for brand feedback. Imagine instant guardrails. Today, your brand voice drifts across 5 freelancers. Imagine one system that remembers."

techniques.primary: Most important information FIRST. Supporting details second. Background last. Reader can stop at any point and has the essential information. Journalism's default. Works for news, announcements, updates, reports.
antiPatterns: Burying the lead — context before conclusion defeats the entire purpose
Equal weight per paragraph — each paragraph should be LESS important than the one before
Using inverted pyramid for persuasion — it is a clarity structure, not a conversion structure

weightResponse.logos > 0.8: pure inverted pyramid — headline, lead, details, context
weightResponse.logos 0.5-0.8: modified inverted pyramid — lead with takeaway, then evidence, then context

techniques.why: AP Stylebook journalism standard. Respects the reader's time and attention. Optimized for scanning — most readers don't finish (Sumo analysis of 650K page hits found only ~20% of readers reach the end; Nielsen found avg reader consumes ~20% of page text).
techniques.example: "Shopify expands AI assistant to all merchants. The tool generates product descriptions, ad copy, and email campaigns from a single brief. [details in decreasing importance]"

techniques.primary: Setup (world + character + tension) → Confrontation (obstacle + stakes) → Resolution. Freytag's pyramid adapted for content marketing. The "character" can be the audience, the brand, a customer, or an idea.
antiPatterns: Setup too long — audience loses patience before the story begins
Stakes unclear — "things were hard" is not stakes, "she'd lose the account" is stakes
Resolution too neat — real stories have rough edges; perfect endings feel fabricated

weightResponse.transportation > 0.8: full three-act — invest in setup, delay resolution, emotional payoff
weightResponse.transportation 0.6-0.8: compressed arc — setup in one beat, focus on confrontation + resolution

techniques.why: Freytag (1863). Stories are the most natural human information structure — we evolved to pay attention to narratives. Transportation (Green & Brock 2000) reduces counter-arguing.
techniques.example: "When Maya launched her bakery, she posted one photo a day. Nobody noticed. Then a food blogger walked in by accident..." [confrontation + resolution follows]

techniques.primary: Narration carries ALL meaning. Visuals are supplementary or absent. Full spoken script with 150 WPM VO density. 150 WPM is the standard voiceover rate (source: National Center for Voice and Speech; confirmed across multiple VO platforms and training resources).
techniques.example: Podcast script, radio ad, audiobook chapter, narration-heavy documentary.

techniques.primary: Narration and visuals SUPPORT each other — same message, different channels. VO explains while screen shows. ~120 WPM density (slower, breathing room for visuals). 80% of marketing video content uses this mode. This is the most common narration mode in marketing video content.
techniques.example: Standard explainer, product overview, corporate brand video.

techniques.primary: Narration and visuals carry DIFFERENT messages that create meaning through juxtaposition. VO tells one story while the screen shows another — the audience constructs the connection. Advanced technique. ~100 WPM density (sparse, each word must earn its place).
techniques.example: Patagonia brand film: serene nature visuals + urgent climate narration. Documentary: upbeat childhood photos + adult voice recounting trauma.

techniques.primary: Visuals carry the message. Narration is sparse or absent. 0-50 WPM. Each word is a deliberate punctuation mark, not explanation. On-screen text may replace spoken narration.
techniques.example: Nike "Just Do It" anthem, Apple keynote product reveal, ASMR, cooking video.

techniques.primary: Invitation, not instruction. "If this resonated, you might enjoy..." Positioned as a natural next step, not a demand. Often embedded in closing content rather than separated as a distinct CTA block.
techniques.example: "Want to see this in action? We'd love to show you." / "Follow for more like this."

techniques.primary: Clear directive with specific action. "Start your free trial." / "Book a demo today." Explicit value proposition in or immediately before the CTA. One CTA per piece — multiple CTAs reduce conversion. Single CTA increased conversion by 266% vs multiple CTAs (source: Campaign Monitor). Hick's Law: decision time increases with number of choices.
techniques.example: "Start editing smarter — free for 14 days. No credit card required."

techniques.primary: Time-bound directive with scarcity. "Limited spots. Closes Friday." Must be REAL scarcity — fabricated urgency destroys trust permanently. Combined with specific consequence of inaction.
antiPatterns: Fake countdown timers — audience knows. Destroys all future credibility.
"Act now!" without a real deadline — generic urgency is noise.
techniques.example: "Early access closes in 48 hours. 200 spots. 140 taken."

techniques.primary: Connective sentence linking two sections. "But here's where it gets interesting." / "And that brings us to the real question." The default — safe, clear, professional.
techniques.whenToUse: Most section transitions. When in doubt, bridge.

techniques.primary: Reference earlier content to connect forward. "Remember the 12-hour problem we mentioned? Here's why it's actually worse than you think." Creates coherence.
techniques.whenToUse: When setup/payoff structure is active. When the piece has planted seeds.

techniques.primary: Strip all ornamentation. After flowing prose, one short declarative sentence. The texture shift IS the emphasis. "That changed everything." Period. New paragraph.
techniques.whenToUse: At the pivot point. When the piece needs to land a single fact with maximum impact.

techniques.primary: End the section with an unanswered question or incomplete thought. Force the audience forward through absence. "And then she opened the envelope." [new section starts WITHOUT revealing what was inside — for 2 more paragraphs]
techniques.whenToUse: When tension is the primary engagement driver. Cliffhanger at section boundary.

techniques.primary: A reveal that RECONTEXTUALIZES everything the audience has read/watched. All prior content takes on new meaning. This is not a twist — it is a deeper truth that was always there, now visible.
antiPatterns: The reveal must be EARNED — planted seeds must exist earlier in the piece
The reveal must be TRUE — fabricated revelations feel like manipulation
Overuse destroys credibility — once per piece maximum, once per campaign is better
techniques.why: Predictive processing violation (Friston 2010) — the brain's prediction model updates retroactively. The emotional impact comes from revising PAST understanding, not just learning something new.
techniques.example: "The reason I know this works is because I was that agency owner. The one who edited every video herself. The 12-hour days were mine."

techniques.primary: Break the fourth wall. Acknowledge the medium. "Yes, this is a marketing video. Yes, we're trying to sell you something. But here's why you should care anyway." Disarms audience defenses through honesty.
antiPatterns: Meta breaks that undermine the entire piece — the break should STRENGTHEN the message
Multiple meta breaks — one is refreshing, two is a gimmick
techniques.why: Deadpool effect — breaking conventions signals confidence and earns trust through vulnerability.
techniques.example: "Look, I know what you're thinking — 'another AI tool.' Stay with me for 30 seconds."

constraints.detection: match against banned phrase list (600+ patterns)
constraints.autoCorrection: replace with brand-appropriate alternative or delete
constraints.why: LLM-generated content has telltale filler: "In today's fast-paced world", "It's important to note that", "Let's dive in", "At the end of the day", "game-changer", "leverage", "unlock", "empower", "cutting-edge", "seamless", "robust", "innovative", "synergy", "circle back"

constraints.detection: standard deviation of sentence word-count < 15% of mean over 10+ sentences
constraints.autoCorrection: flag for rewrite with rhythm variation target
constraints.why: LLMs produce metronomically uniform sentences. Human writers vary naturally. See Part 2: rhythmic_variation signal.

constraints.detection: opening matches common LLM patterns: "In today's...", "Have you ever...", "What if I told you...", "Did you know that..."
constraints.autoCorrection: rewrite opener using selected hook technique from Part 4
constraints.why: Trained audiences (especially marketing professionals) detect these instantly.

constraints.detection: all paragraphs within ±20% of same length for 5+ consecutive paragraphs
constraints.autoCorrection: flag for structural variation
constraints.why: LLMs produce uniform paragraph blocks. Human writers vary paragraph length deliberately — short punch paragraphs, long development paragraphs.

constraints.detection: >3 hedge phrases per 200 words ("it seems", "perhaps", "might", "could potentially")
constraints.autoCorrection: strengthen claims or remove hedges, per certainty signal
constraints.why: LLMs over-hedge to seem balanced. Real writers commit to their claims. Exception: certainty < 0.4 (deliberately provisional content is exempt)

constraints.detection: >40% of content is bulleted/numbered lists
constraints.autoCorrection: convert some lists to prose
constraints.why: LLMs default to lists as a crutch. Lists are a valid formatting tool (Part 4 atlas) but content that is MOSTLY lists reads as outline, not finished work.

constraints.detection: >4 formal transition words per 300 words ("furthermore", "moreover", "additionally", "consequently", "nevertheless", "in conclusion")
constraints.autoCorrection: remove or replace with natural connective language
constraints.why: LLMs over-use academic transition words. Real writers use implicit transitions, conjunctions, or white space — not a thesaurus of "moreover."

constraints.detection: 3+ instances of exactly-three-item lists or "three reasons/tips/steps" in one piece
constraints.autoCorrection: flag — vary list lengths (2, 4, 5, 7 are all valid)
constraints.why: LLMs almost always generate exactly 3 examples. The "rule of three" is real but when EVERY list has exactly 3 items, it signals AI generation.

constraints.detection: pattern: "While X, it's also true that Y" or "On one hand... on the other hand" appearing 2+ times in one piece
constraints.autoCorrection: flag for rewrite — commit to a position or acknowledge complexity without formula
constraints.why: LLMs hedge by presenting both sides in a formulaic pattern. Real writers who genuinely see both sides express it with nuance, not with "on the other hand."

constraints.detection: final paragraph restates 3+ key points already made in the piece, using similar phrasing
constraints.autoCorrection: flag — replace with forward-looking close, CTA, or callback (Part 4 closing techniques)
constraints.why: The trademark LLM ending: "In summary, we've covered X, Y, and Z." Real writers end with resonance, not recitation. If the reader needs a summary, the piece was too long.

constraints.detection: content length exceeds platform maximum
constraints.autoCorrection: trim content, prioritizing removal of lowest-weight scenes/sections
constraints.platforms: see Part 8 for exact limits per platform

constraints.detection: video script duration (word count / WPM) exceeds platform maximum
constraints.autoCorrection: flag excess scenes for user review
constraints.platforms: see Part 8 for exact duration limits

constraints.detection: first substantive hook element appears after platform-specific threshold TikTok: 3 seconds. Instagram Reels: 3 seconds. YouTube: 10 seconds. LinkedIn: first 210 characters (desktop) / 140 characters (mobile)
constraints.autoCorrection: restructure to front-load hook
constraints.why: each platform has a measured attention threshold — content that doesn't hook within it gets zero algorithmic distribution

constraints.detection: word count / duration exceeds comfortable WPM for format Video narration: > 170 WPM (uncomfortable VO pace) Presentation: > 160 WPM (speaker can't keep up) Podcast: > 190 WPM (listener fatigue) ⚠️ WPM thresholds are industry standards confirmed across VO training resources. Standard VO: 150 WPM. Fast: 170-180 WPM. Slow: 120-130 WPM.
constraints.autoCorrection: flag excess words for trim or increase target_length

constraints.detection: cognitive_load (derived) > 0.8 AND negative_space < 0.2
constraints.autoCorrection: add section breaks, whitespace, or simplify language
constraints.why: Sweller's cognitive load theory — intrinsic load + extraneous load must not exceed working memory capacity. Dense content without breathing room overwhelms.

constraints.detection: deterministic string matching against Brand DNA kill list (Part 1)
constraints.autoCorrection: replace with preferred alternative from vocabulary hierarchy

constraints.detection: output signal values exceed Brand DNA tone guardrails (Part 1)
constraints.autoCorrection: flag for rewrite with adjusted signal targets

constraints.detection: named competitor detected in output (requires competitor list in Brand DNA)
constraints.autoCorrection: remove mention or replace with generic reference per competitor_policy

constraints.detection: Flesch-Kincaid grade level exceeds reading_level_target by > 2 grades
constraints.autoCorrection: simplify vocabulary and sentence structure
constraints.why: content that exceeds the audience's reading comfort level gets abandoned. Grade 8 = mass consumer. Grade 12 = professional. Grade 16+ = academic. ⚠️ Flesch-Kincaid is a proxy — it measures syntax complexity, not conceptual difficulty.

constraints.detection: >5% of words are domain-specific jargon AND assumed_expertise < 0.5
constraints.autoCorrection: flag jargon words, suggest plain-language alternatives
constraints.why: jargon is a barrier for non-expert audiences. It is CORRECT for expert audiences (in_group_signal > 0.7) — this constraint is suppressed when expertise is high.

constraints.detection: regulatory_profile requires disclosures AND output does not contain them
constraints.autoCorrection: append required disclosure text (system flags location, human writes disclosure)

constraints.detection: output contains claim type banned by regulatory_profile Pharma: cure/prevent/treat claims without FDA-approved indications Finance: guaranteed returns, specific performance predictions Alcohol: health benefits, targeting minors
constraints.autoCorrection: remove claim, flag for human rewrite

constraints.detection: superlatives ("best", "fastest", "most effective", "#1") in regulated content
constraints.autoCorrection: remove superlative, replace with qualified claim
constraints.why: regulated industries (pharma, finance) ban superlatives unless substantiated

constraints.detection: numeric claim (percentage, count, monetary value) without source attribution
constraints.autoCorrection: flag claim, require user to provide source or remove
constraints.why: AI-fabricated statistics are the #1 credibility risk. Every number must trace to user-provided material (Part 0, section 0.8).

constraints.detection: quote attributed to a named person/company not in user-provided materials
constraints.autoCorrection: remove quote, flag for user
constraints.why: fabricated testimonials are FTC violations (US) and ASA violations (UK) regardless of industry

constraints.detection: claim that cannot be verified from user-provided materials (e.g., "industry-leading", "best-in-class", "revolutionary")
constraints.autoCorrection: replace with specific, verifiable claim or remove

platforms.name: TikTok
platforms.raw:
Last verified: 2026-05-19
Sources: flowshorts.app, socialrails.com, TikTok official docs

Character limits:
  Caption: 4,000 characters (expanded from 2,200 in 2024)
  Bio: 80 characters
  Username: 24 characters

Duration limits:
  Minimum: 3 seconds
  In-app recording: up to 10 minutes
  Uploaded video: up to 60 minutes
  Algorithm sweet spot: 21-34 seconds (entertainment), 45-75 seconds (informative)
  Source: socialrails.com 2026, retensis.com 2026

Aspect ratio:
  Preferred: 9:16 (vertical, full-screen)
  Accepted: 1:1, 16:9
  Vertical vs horizontal: 9x completion rate for vertical (source: Snapchat/Kleiner Perkins 2015)

Algorithm signals (ranked by weight):
  1. Completion rate (strongest — videos with >50% avg completion get significantly more distribution)
  2. Rewatch rate
  3. Share rate (especially DM shares)
  4. Comment rate
  5. Like rate (weakest of the engagement signals)
  Source: socialync.io 2026, various industry analyses

Hook threshold: 3 seconds — <60% retention at 3s = minimal algorithmic push

platforms.name: Instagram
platforms.raw:
Last verified: 2026-05-19
Sources: zeely.ai, heytrendy.app, Instagram official docs

Reels duration:
  Minimum: 3 seconds
  Maximum: 20 minutes (expanded from 90 seconds in 2024)
  Algorithm favors: under 90 seconds for organic discovery
  Sweet spot: 7-15 seconds (reach), 15-60 seconds (tutorials), 3+ minutes (conversion, followers only)

Feed post caption: 2,200 characters
  Visible before fold: ~125 characters
  Desktop: ~210 characters before "more"

Stories: 60 seconds per story (previously 15s segments)

Algorithm signals:
  1. DM shares (#1 signal per Instagram head Adam Mosseri)
  2. Saves
  3. Comments
  4. Likes
  5. Watch time (Reels)

Hashtags: max 30, optimal 3-5 (keywords > hashtags in 2026)

platforms.name: LinkedIn
platforms.raw:
Last verified: 2026-05-19
Sources: authoredup.com, connectsafely.ai, LinkedIn official docs

Post character limit: 3,000 characters
  Optimal engagement: 1,300-1,900 characters (source: analysis of 10,000+ posts, connectsafely.ai)
  Visible before fold: ~210 characters (desktop), ~140 characters (mobile)

Article character limit: 125,000 characters (~40,000 words)

Video duration:
  Feed: 3 seconds to 10 minutes
  Optimal: 30-90 seconds

Algorithm signals:
  1. Dwell time (time spent reading/viewing)
  2. Engagement velocity (speed of initial reactions)
  3. Comment depth (substantive > emoji)
  4. Shares to network
  5. Completion rate (video)

Carousel: up to 300 slides (PDF format), optimal 6-10 slides
  Carousel engagement: 6.6% average (highest format engagement on LinkedIn)

platforms.name: YouTube
platforms.raw:
Last verified: 2026-05-19

Shorts:
  Duration: 3 seconds to 3 minutes
  Aspect: 9:16 (vertical)
  Sweet spot: 30-60 seconds

Long-form:
  Maximum: 12 hours (default), 256 GB file size
  Sweet spot: 8-12 minutes (ad mid-roll eligible at 8 min)

Title: 100 characters (optimal 60-70 for full display)
Description: 5,000 characters

Algorithm signals:
  1. Click-through rate (thumbnail + title)
  2. Average view duration (watch time)
  3. Session time (does your video lead to more YouTube watching?)
  4. Engagement (likes, comments, shares)

Thumbnail: 1280x720 pixels, <2MB

Post: 280 characters (free), 25,000 characters (Premium)

  Threads generate 63% more impressions than single posts

Video: up to 2 hours 20 minutes (free), up to 4 hours (Premium)

platforms.name: Email

Subject line: optimal 30-50 characters (6-10 words)
